title: What brings you into our corner of the university?
prompt: First, what brings you into our corner of the university?

options.text: 🌱 I could see English becoming a big part of my undergraduate degree.
🧩 I'd like to add more English to what I'm already studying.
🎓 I'm looking beyond the bachelor's degree.
➕ I'm already a graduate student somewhere else.
🧭 I have absolutely no idea yet. That's why I clicked this thing.

purpose: Soft credential/commitment routing only; no intellectual score.

title: Free afternoon
prompt: You get a free afternoon. Which rabbit hole could steal two hours?

options.text: 🗣️ Why does everybody around here pronounce that differently?
📚 A book sends me down a historical rabbit hole.
✍️ Something happened this morning that would make a great story.
💬 An argument online makes me fascinated by how it is persuading people.
🌎 I hear someone switching between languages and wonder what is happening.

title: Two tabs
prompt: Two tabs are allowed. Which ones are you opening? Pick up to two.

options.text: 🗣️ Why people have different accents
📜 A bizarre moment in history
👶 Are babies secretly language-learning supercomputers?
✍️ How a great writer pulled off that sentence
📱 Why everyone suddenly talks about something the same way
📰 How something goes from draft to published

title: Oddly satisfying
prompt: Which sounds most oddly satisfying?

options.text: ✂️ Cutting 200 unnecessary words
🔍 Finding a pattern nobody noticed
🧩 Making something complicated make sense
📚 Realizing two wildly different books are secretly talking to each other
🗣️ Hearing an accent and wondering where it came from
✍️ Getting one paragraph exactly right

title: Fix one thing
prompt: Which of these would bother you enough that you'd actually want to fix it?

options.text: 📝 Instructions that make a simple task impossible.
✍️ A fascinating story told badly. There's something good in there.
🎓 Someone who understands something but cannot explain it to students.
📖 An interpretation of a book that completely ignores its historical context.
🗣️ Someone saying another person's way of speaking is “wrong.”

title: Choose your superpower
prompt: You get one suspiciously specific superpower. Keep one.

options.text: 🎯 Know exactly what an audience needs to hear
🧠 See the hidden mental process behind language
📚 See every text in its historical and cultural web
✍️ Turn lived experience into a story people cannot stop reading
👩‍🏫 Find the explanation that finally makes something click
🔎 Spot the evidence everyone else missed

purpose: Clean forced-choice discriminator; one answer alone can never establish confidence.

title: Language gets interesting when...
prompt: Language gets most interesting when...

options.text: 🧠 ...it meets the mind. How do we process sounds, sentences, jokes, and sarcasm?
👥 ...it meets society. Accents, dialects, identity, judgment, change.
🌎 ...languages meet each other. Learning, mixing, switching, moving between languages.
📝 ...it becomes text. Why does one wording work better for an audience?
🔬 ...someone realizes we can collect data about all of this.

title: I don't have an accent.
prompt: Someone says: “I don't have an accent.” Your brain:

options.text: 😂 Oh, you absolutely do.
🗺️ Okay, but where did you grow up?
👥 Interesting that some accents get noticed and others do not.
🔬 Can I record you? For science.
😌 My brain has no response to this information.

purpose: Sociolinguistic/phonetic orientation with a zero-point fun option.

title: Two languages, one mind
prompt: A bilingual speaker knows the word they want - but the other language gets there first. What makes you curious?

options.text: 🧠 What just happened in their mind?
🌎 When and why does one language become easier to access than another?
👥 Would this change depending on who they are talking to?
🎓 How does this affect learning or teaching another language?
✍️ How could a writer represent that multilingual experience on the page?

title: The mystery phrase
prompt: A phrase suddenly seems to be everywhere - except among people twenty years older. You get one question answered.

options.text: 🧭 Where did it come from?
👥 Why did this group adopt it?
📈 How is its meaning changing?
⚖️ Why do some people hate hearing it?
🧠 How does a brain learn a new meaning for an old word?

title: Linguistic detective
prompt: Pick your evidence. Up to two.

options.text: 🎙️ Recordings
💬 Conversations
🧠 Experiments
📱 Social media
📝 Written texts
🌎 Multilingual speakers

title: Words doing things
prompt: Two messages say the same thing. One persuades people; the other falls flat. What do you want to know?

options.text: 🎯 Who each message imagined its audience to be
🧱 How the argument was structured
🗣️ Which wording choices changed the effect
🌎 What cultural assumptions the messages relied on
🧪 How we could test which version actually works

title: The unfamiliar text
prompt: You open a text you've never read. What makes you lean in?

options.text: 🔍 Something strange is happening in the writing itself. I want to work out what it is doing.
🕰️ This text came from another world. I want the history and culture around it.
🌍 Whose perspective are we getting - and whose are we not?
🔗 It reminds me of something happening now.
✍️ I am noticing techniques I could steal. Respectfully.

title: The old book
prompt: You find a 150-year-old book with somebody's notes in the margins. What is most interesting?

options.text: 📖 The book
✏️ The notes
🕰️ The person who wrote the notes
🌎 The world they were living in
👀 Why am I being forced to choose?

title: Whose story?
prompt: A story is celebrated as “universal.” What question are you most tempted to ask?

options.text: 🌎 Universal for whom?
🗣️ Whose voice sounds “normal” in this story?
🕰️ Would readers in another time have seen it that way?
🔍 What in the text makes people read it as universal?
✍️ How would the story change if somebody else told it?

purpose: Identity, perspective, historical reception, textual analysis.

title: Borrow a time machine
prompt: You get ONE literary field trip.

options.text: 🏰 Medieval world
🎭 Shakespeare's London
🕯️ Nineteenth century
🗽 Twentieth-century America
🌎 Somewhere shaped by colonialism and its aftermath
🚀 Actually, take me back to the present

purpose: Low-weight flavor question for course/faculty hooks.

title: The family story
prompt: You learn something remarkable about someone in your family. Nobody agrees on exactly what happened. What pulls you in?

options.text: ✍️ I can already see the opening scene.
🎙️ Start interviewing everybody before their versions disappear.
🗃️ Find letters, photographs, records - what actually happened?
🌎 Zoom out: what does this tell us about their time, place, or community?
🧠 Why do people remember the same event differently?

graduate_variant.prompt: You inherit an archive of contradictory accounts around one life/event. What becomes the project?

title: I have a story about that.
prompt: “I have a story about that.” Your reaction:

options.text: ✍️ Tell it.
🔍 Research it.
🎙️ Interview someone.
🧠 Figure out why you remember it that way.
😬 Maybe take that one to the grave.

purpose: Fast CNF orientation with a breathing-room answer.

title: Truth gets messy
prompt: You are writing about a real event, and the facts resist the neat version of the story. What sounds most interesting?

options.text: 🧭 Let the messiness become part of the form.
🔎 Keep digging until I understand the contradictions.
🎙️ Put different people's versions into conversation.
⚖️ Think hard about what I owe the real people in the story.
✂️ Find the clearest truthful version without flattening it.

title: The broken draft
prompt: Someone sends you a draft and says, “Something isn't working.” What sounds satisfying?

options.text: ✂️ Find the sentence doing absolutely nothing and delete it.
🧭 Figure out what the piece is really trying to become.
👀 Think about the reader: where will they get confused, bored, persuaded, surprised?
📰 Think beyond the draft: where does this belong and how do we get it to readers?
🏃 Pretend I never received the file.

title: Hit publish
prompt: What is the most satisfying moment?

options.text: ✍️ Writing it
✂️ Making it better
📰 Choosing what gets published
🎨 Figuring out how readers experience it
🚀 Sending it into the world

title: Your nemesis appears: ASSEMBLY REQUIRED
prompt: The instructions are terrible. You:

options.text: 🛠️ Rewrite them.
🖼️ Add visuals.
🧪 Watch someone try them and see where they fail.
🤬 Complain about them while assembling it incorrectly.

title: The audience problem
prompt: You have one complicated idea and three audiences: experts, new students, and the public. What sounds fun?

options.text: 🎯 Rebuild the explanation for each audience.
🧩 Find the one analogy that works across all three.
📐 Decide what each audience needs first, second, and never.
🧪 Test versions and see what people actually understand.
✍️ Make all three versions sound good, not merely correct.

graduate_variant.prompt: A team hands you a substantial project and says: We know what we mean; we do not know how to communicate it.

title: Make this usable
prompt: A page is technically accurate but nobody can use it. Pick up to two things you want to fix first.

options.text: 🧭 Organization
✂️ Wordiness
🎨 Visual hierarchy
🎯 Audience mismatch
🧪 Whether users can actually complete the task

title: Imagine you discover you love teaching
prompt: Suppose you find that you enjoy teaching. Where can you picture yourself?

options.text: 🏫 An English classroom: literature, writing, language - middle or high school.
🌎 A multilingual classroom: helping people develop English while learning how languages work.
🧠 Somewhere people are figuring things out: tutoring, mentoring, maybe college.
🔬 Wait - can I study learning instead? I am as interested in how people acquire/use language as teaching it.
😅 You lost me at “discover that you love teaching.” Respectfully, no.

purpose: Distinguish Secondary English, TESOL, pedagogy, and language research.

title: They still don't get it
prompt: You've explained something twice. They still don't get it.

options.text: 🔄 Explain it differently.
🧩 Break it into pieces.
👂 Ask what part is not clicking.
🔍 Become fascinated by why it is not clicking.
🏃 I was not built for this scenario.

title: Study learning instead
prompt: Suppose you could spend a semester studying one learning mystery. Which one?

options.text: 🌎 Why some ways of learning another language work better than others
🧠 How people process and retrieve language in real time
✍️ How writers learn through feedback and revision
👥 How classroom identities and communities shape participation
📚 How people learn to interpret difficult texts

title: One practical question
prompt: One practical question: which of these sounds closest to what you’re exploring?

options.text: 🏫 I teach—or plan to teach—high school English, including dual enrollment.
📚 I teach high school English, but I’m looking more broadly at graduate English study.
🧑‍🏫 I’m interested in teaching, but not specifically in dual/concurrent enrollment.
🎓 I’m mainly here to explore graduate English study beyond the teaching question.

purpose: Establish the specific professional context needed before surfacing the English Dual Enrollment Certificate; do not score intellectual interests.

title: Choose an artifact
prompt: You have to investigate ONE ordinary thing as if it were an artifact from another civilization. Pick it.

options.text: 📱 A week of TikToks
📣 An advertisement
👗 A fashion trend
🎵 A song everyone suddenly knows
🗣️ A phrase people your age use that older people do not
📖 A bestselling novel

purpose: Wildcard; choice lightly scores, follow-up does the diagnostic work.

title: Academic dinner party
prompt: You arrive late. One seat is left at each table. Where are you sitting?

options.text: 📚 People arguing about what a famous book actually means
🗣️ People comparing accents and telling language stories
✍️ People swapping unbelievable true stories
🧠 People debating why language changes across groups and generations
🛠️ People redesigning the menu because apparently that became the evening project
😈 The table with the best gossip. Obviously.

title: One question forever
prompt: One question gets to follow you around forever. Which one?

options.text: 🔍 What is really going on here?
🌎 How did culture/history/power shape this?
🗣️ Why do people use language this way?
📚 What else can this text mean?
✍️ How can I make this truer, sharper, or more alive on the page?
🎯 How can I make this work better for the people who need it?
🎓 How can I help someone else understand this?

graduate_variant.prompt: You receive protected time to pursue one family of questions for a year. Which sounds least exhausting?

title: You keep coming back to language...
prompt: Which mystery would you most want answered?

options.text: 🧠 Why are some aspects of language automatic while others take work?
👥 Why do people change how they speak around different people?
🌎 What actually happens while someone learns another language?
🎙️ What makes an accent sound like that?
📈 How does a new way of speaking spread?
💬 How does wording change what people believe?

title: Okay, the story got complicated.
prompt: Your sources disagree. Good news or bad news?

options.text: ✨ Good news. That disagreement is part of the story.
🔎 Bad news. I need to establish what happened.
🧠 Interesting news. Why do they remember it differently?
⚖️ Complicated news. What can I responsibly say about real people?

title: You are not done with that text yet.
prompt: What pulls you further in?

options.text: 🕰️ The historical world around it
🔍 The writer's formal choices
🌎 Gender, race, class, empire, or social expectations
👥 What readers at the time thought
🔗 How we would read it differently now

title: Apparently unusable information bothers you.
prompt: Which part of “make it better” sounds best?

options.text: 🎯 Understand the audience
🧭 Restructure the information
✂️ Edit the language
🎨 Redesign how people encounter it
🧪 Test it with real users

title: Teaching keeps sneaking into your answers...
prompt: What is the satisfying part?

options.text: 💡 The moment something clicks
🧩 Designing a better way to explain it
👂 Learning how another person thinks
🌎 Working across languages/cultures
🔬 Studying why learning succeeds or fails

title: Okay. What do you want to know about it?
prompt: Okay. What do you want to know about it?

options.text: 🕰️ Where it came from and how it got here
🎯 Who it is trying to reach or persuade
🌎 What it says about identity, culture, or power
🗣️ How its language is changing or doing social work
🔍 How its form/structure makes it work
📣 Why people keep sharing, reading, or repeating it

purpose: Wildcard follow-up; turns artifact choice into a diagnostic orientation.

title: Pick a setting
prompt: Where would you most happily spend an hour?

options.text: ☕ Coffee shop with a notebook
📚 Library stacks
🎙️ Language lab
📰 Editorial room
🏫 Classroom
🌳 Somewhere outside with something to read

title: Pick your evidence aesthetic
prompt: Which pile on a desk looks most irresistible?

options.text: 📜 Old letters and marginal notes
🎧 Headphones + waveforms
📝 A draft covered in edits
📊 A tiny dataset begging for a pattern
📚 Three books that should not belong together but somehow do
